newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil spells out rewrite of pension reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Brazil spells out rewrite of pension reform bill.

text.p: Brazilian Social Security Minister Reinhold Stephanes met Tuesday with a senator in charge of a pension reform bill to explain key points the government wants restored to its text, a ministry spokeswoman said.

"We urgently need this bill to be approved," the spokeswoman said after the minister met with Sen. Benavides Veras, recalling how Brazil's social security system posted a deficit of roughly $500 million in 1996.
The government wants to overhaul the social security system, principally by tieing pensions to contributions and scrapping privileges for civil servants.
But its attempts to approve the controversial reform have so far proved disastrous.
The Chamber of Deputies last spring rejected a first draft of the bill and then in July stripped a revised version of many of its main points, rendering it virtually useless.
Now the government wants the Senate to rewrite the bill to include the following proposals:
-- a minimum retirement age for public sector workers of 60 for men and 55 for women, rising to 65 and 60 respectively within ten years;
-- an end to automatic increases in the value of public sector pensions to match salary raises;

-- a ceiling of 8,500 reais a month on the amount of pay and pensions public sector workers may receive. A proposal for a 10,800-real a month ceiling is also a central plank of in the government's civil service reform. Officials say the level of the ceiling will depend on whichever reform is approved first;
-- a ban on civil servants accumulating several special pensions, awarded after a few years of service, throughout their careers;

-- an end to special pensions for university professors, many of whom are currently able to retire by the time they are 40, draining universities of their most qualified staff and adding to payroll costs.
The ministry spokeswoman said the government expected Senator Veras to produce a draft of the revised bill within two months.
It would then require two three-fifths majorities on the floor of the Senate before returning to the Chamber of Deputies for approval of the new-look text.
